Chapter One: A World on the Edge—Ordinary Lives Before the Storm.
Imagine waking up in Kraków, before everything changed. The city hums with familiar sounds—trams rattling by, kids rushing off to school, shopkeepers sweeping their doorsteps. For so many Jewish families, life is about the little routines: cooking together, running small businesses, sharing stories and laughter at the dinner table. There’s this real sense of belonging, even if you sometimes hear uneasy news from outside.
At first, the idea of violence or war feels far away—almost like a distant rumor. Most folks hope, maybe even believe, that the trouble won’t reach them. Some have seen hard times before and figure, if they just wait it out, things will settle down. But then, the German army arrives. Suddenly, soldiers in strange uniforms are everywhere, and with them come new rules: curfews, restrictions, and slowly, rights begin to disappear.
People try to adjust as best they can. Picture a tailor, focusing on each stitch just to block out worry, or a baker quietly counting how much flour is left. Parents do their best to reassure their kids, though deep down, they’re nervous too—feeling the world shift under their feet. The tight-knit community that once brought comfort is now shadowed by fear. Neighbors who used to celebrate together start looking at each other with suspicion, unsure of who they can really trust.
Right in the midst of all this, a new face shows up—Oskar Schindler. He’s a businessman from the Sudetenland, full of charm and quick to make friends. At first glance, he seems like just another guy hoping to cash in during tough times. He’s clever, always looking for the next opportunity.
But as things grow more dangerous for Kraków’s Jewish community, those clear lines between friend and foe start to blur. Some people, driven by fear or greed, turn their backs on neighbors. Yet others, quietly and often at great risk, find small ways to help—maybe sharing a loaf of bread, offering a place to hide, or just listening when someone needs to talk. In moments like these, it becomes clear: the choices people make, even the ones nobody else sees, can change everything—not just for themselves, but for everyone around them.
Those early days under occupation are filled with uncertainty and denial. Many hold on, hoping the worst won’t actually happen. But as the machine of oppression keeps moving, everyone is forced to face a new, colder reality. The world they knew is fading, replaced by something far more dangerous. It’s in this uncertain place that both cruelty and compassion take root—setting the stage for tragedies we can barely imagine, and for acts of courage that will never be forgotten.
